Telehealth visit by telephone (audio only). The patient confirmed his identity verbally and agreed to a phone visit. No visual examination was possible.

This is a 47-year-old male with sickle cell disease who called with 2 days of pain in his low back and both thighs, which he says feels like his usual crisis pain and reaches 8 out of 10 at worst. He takes hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily. He tried his leftover oxycodone 5 mg every 4 hours as needed at home with little relief. He reports heavy alcohol use, about 6 beers daily, with his last drink yesterday evening. He denies fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and leg swelling. His home thermometer read 98.9 F this morning. He is speaking in full sentences and sounds uncomfortable but not short of breath.

Impression: sickle cell disease with an acute pain crisis that is not controlled at home, with heavy alcohol use as a contributing concern. He will go to the day infusion unit today for IV fluids and IV pain medicine, with a CBC, reticulocyte count, and metabolic panel on arrival. Continue hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily. I advised him to stop drinking alcohol, especially while taking oxycodone, and to drink plenty of water. He should go to the emergency department for fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Hematology follow-up in 1 week.
summary: A 47-year-old man with sickle cell disease and heavy alcohol use contacted the clinic by telephone with 2 days of low back and thigh pain like his usual crisis pain, rated 8 out of 10 at worst, with little relief from home oxycodone while taking hydroxyurea. He denied fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and leg swelling. The clinician assessed an acute pain crisis that is not controlled at home. He was sent to the day infusion unit for IV fluids, IV pain medicine, and blood tests, told to continue hydroxyurea and stop drinking alcohol, given return precautions, and arranged hematology follow-up in 1 week.

This is a dictation for a follow-up visit in the psychiatry specialty clinic. The patient is a 40-year-old female with post-traumatic stress disorder after a serious car crash about 2 years ago, along with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and obesity. She has limited health literacy and says that medical words and pill names are confusing, so I used plain language and teach-back throughout the visit.

History of present illness. She reports that nightmares are still happening about four nights a week and that she wakes up sweating and cannot get back to sleep. She has flashbacks when she hears loud braking noises, she avoids driving on the highway, and she feels jumpy and on edge most days. She also reports low mood and irritability. She says the trazodone makes her groggy in the morning and she nearly missed her bus twice. She denies suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, and hallucinations. She denies alcohol use and any drug use.

Medications. She says she takes sertraline 100 mg every morning, correction, she brought the bottle with her and the label reads 50 mg every morning, so her current dose is sertraline 50 mg daily. She takes trazodone 50 mg at bedtime. She takes metformin 500 mg twice a day and amlodipine 5 mg daily, and since she is unsure of the names I went through each bottle with her. She has no known drug allergies.

Exam. Blood pressure 138/84, HR 92, and BMI 34. On mental status exam she is casually dressed and cooperative with fair eye contact, speech is normal in rate, mood is described as tired and on edge, affect is anxious, thought process is linear, and there is no evidence of psychosis. Insight and judgment are fair.

Data. PCL-5 score today was 52 and PHQ-9 score was 14. Her TSH last month was 2.1 and her hemoglobin A1c was 7.1 percent.

Impression. Post-traumatic stress disorder with persistent nightmares and hyperarousal and only a partial response to a low dose of sertraline, with comorbid depressive symptoms and daytime sedation from trazodone. Her diabetes is reasonably controlled and her blood pressure is acceptable.

For the plan, one, increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg every morning. Two, discontinue trazodone because of the morning grogginess. Three, start prazosin 1 mg at bedtime for the nightmares, with instructions to stand up slowly because it can cause dizziness, and I will consider increasing to 2 mg at the next visit if she tolerates it. Four, continue metformin 500 mg twice a day and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Five, because of her health literacy I wrote one-page instructions in large print with a picture of each pill, marked the morning and bedtime boxes on her pill organizer, and used teach-back, and she was able to repeat the changes correctly. Six, refer her to cognitive processing therapy for trauma and to the clinic social worker for help with transportation. Seven, repeat the PCL-5 and PHQ-9 and a basic metabolic panel at the next visit. Return in 4 weeks, sooner if she has any thoughts of hurting herself.
summary: A 40-year-old woman with post-traumatic stress disorder after a car crash, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and obesity presented for psychiatry follow-up with persistent nightmares, flashbacks, feeling jumpy and on edge, low mood, and irritability, plus morning grogginess from trazodone. She denied suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, and hallucinations, and her PCL-5 score was 52 and PHQ-9 score was 14. Her sertraline dose was corrected to 50 mg daily from the bottle label. Because of limited health literacy, the clinician used plain language and teach-back, increased sertraline to 100 mg every morning, stopped trazodone, started prazosin 1 mg at bedtime, and arranged therapy, social work, and follow-up in 4 weeks.

Doctor: Hello, thanks for coming in. I have you down as an 83-year-old female with a kidney transplant. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. I had the transplant about ten years ago. My transplant clinic is closed today and I just wanted someone to check that everything is okay.
Doctor: Any fever, or burning when you pass urine?
Patient: No fever, no burning.
Doctor: Any pain over the transplant, here on the lower right side of your belly?
Patient: No pain there.
Doctor: Are you passing your usual amount of urine? Any swelling in the legs?
Patient: Same as always. No swelling.
Doctor: Which medicines do you take?
Patient: Tacrolimus 1 mg twice a day and prednisone 5 mg every morning.
Doctor: Any missed doses lately?
Patient: No, I use a pill box.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure is 126/74, pulse 72, temperature 98.2, and oxygen is 97% on room air. Your lungs are clear, there is no swelling in your ankles, and the transplant site is not tender. The urine dipstick is negative for blood and protein.
Patient: That sounds good.
Doctor: My impression is that your kidney transplant is stable, with no sign of infection or rejection today. Keep taking the tacrolimus and the prednisone at the same doses. I am sending blood work today, a creatinine and a tacrolimus level, and please call your transplant clinic tomorrow to schedule a visit this week. If you get a fever, pass less urine, notice swelling, or have pain over the transplant, come back right away.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: An 83-year-old woman with a kidney transplant from about ten years ago came to urgent care for a check because her transplant clinic was closed. She denied fever, burning with urination, pain over the transplant, and leg swelling, and she takes tacrolimus and prednisone without missed doses. Vital signs were unremarkable, the transplant site was not tender, and the urine dipstick was negative for blood and protein. The clinician judged the transplant stable with no sign of infection or rejection, continued both medicines, ordered a creatinine and tacrolimus level, and advised a transplant clinic visit this week with return precautions.

Doctor: Good afternoon. I am using a professional Spanish interpreter for our visit, so I will pause after each sentence. I understand you are a 21-year-old female with psoriatic arthritis and a swollen finger. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. My right index finger has been swollen and painful for about five days. It looks like a sausage. In the morning it is stiff for more than an hour.
Doctor: Any injury to the hand?
Patient: No, no injury.
Doctor: Any fever, or any redness or pain in your eyes?
Patient: No fever, and my eyes are fine.
Doctor: What medicines do you take for the arthritis?
Patient: Methotrexate 15 mg once a week and folic acid 1 mg every day. I have also been taking ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times a day from the pharmacy, but it barely helps.
Doctor: How is the skin?
Patient: The patches on my elbows and scalp are about the same.
Doctor: Methotrexate is not safe in pregnancy. Are you using birth control?
Patient: Yes, I have an IUD.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure is 112/70, pulse 78, and temperature 98.4. The whole right index finger is swollen, which we call dactylitis, and it is tender over the middle joint. You also have scaly psoriatic plaques on both elbows. The urine pregnancy test we did today is negative. The X-ray of your right hand shows soft tissue swelling around the middle joint but no fracture and no erosions. Your CRP from last week was 14 mg/L, which is mildly high.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: This is a flare of your psoriatic arthritis. Please keep taking the methotrexate and the folic acid. Stop the ibuprofen and start naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 10 days. Call your rheumatologist tomorrow and ask to be seen this week, because you may need a stronger medicine. Come back or go to the emergency room if you get a fever, a red painful eye, or you cannot use the hand.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 21-year-old woman with psoriatic arthritis, seen through a professional Spanish interpreter at urgent care, had 5 days of a swollen, painful right index finger with morning stiffness lasting over an hour. She denied fever and eye redness or pain, and she was taking methotrexate, folic acid, and ibuprofen with little relief. Vital signs were unremarkable, the urine pregnancy test was negative, the hand X-ray showed soft tissue swelling without fracture or erosions, and CRP was 14 mg/L. The clinician diagnosed a flare of psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis, continued methotrexate and folic acid, replaced ibuprofen with naproxen 500 mg twice a day, and advised rheumatology follow-up this week.

Hospital day 3 for this 87-year-old male admitted with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, and a ground-level fall without injury, in the setting of progressive unintentional weight loss. His daughter, who is his primary caregiver and lives with him, is at the bedside and provides much of the history because the patient has mild dementia and has difficulty recalling details.

Overnight he slept well and had no falls, no fever, and no vomiting. This morning he reports poor appetite and feeling tired, and he says he gets lightheaded when he stands up. The daughter first reported that he had lost about 10 pounds over 3 months. After reviewing the clinic weights she brought from home, she clarified that he has actually lost 22 pounds over 6 months, from 168 pounds to 146 pounds, which is about 13 percent of his body weight. She says he eats about half of each meal and now needs help with bathing and meals. He denies difficulty swallowing, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, black or bloody stools, cough, night sweats, and chest pain. The daughter denies any choking with meals.

His history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, BPH, and mild dementia. Home medications were reviewed with the daughter. She first stated that he takes lisinopril 5 mg daily, but the pharmacy list she brought confirms lisinopril 20 mg daily. He also takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, and donepezil 5 mg daily.

On examination his temperature is 97.9 F, heart rate 76 and irregular, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 96% on room air. Blood pressure is 104/62 sitting and 88/54 standing. Weight is 66 kg. He is thin and frail-appearing with temporal wasting, and his mucous membranes are slightly dry. His dentures fit poorly. Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular without a murmur, the lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. He walks slowly with a walker, grip strength is weak, and his Clinical Frailty Scale score is 6.

Labs show sodium 138, potassium 4.4, creatinine 1.6 with an eGFR of 38, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, WBC 7.2, albumin 2.9, TSH 1.8, and hemoglobin A1c 6.4 percent. Chest x-ray shows no mass. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no mass or lymphadenopathy. The speech therapy swallow evaluation found no aspiration.

Frailty with unintentional weight loss, which is likely multifactorial: reduced appetite, poorly fitting dentures, mild dementia, and polypharmacy, with no malignancy found on imaging so far. He also has orthostatic hypotension, likely worsened by lisinopril and poor intake. Chronic kidney disease limits metformin use.

For the weight loss, I am starting mirtazapine 7.5 mg at bedtime to help appetite and sleep, adding an oral nutrition supplement twice daily between meals, and requesting a dietitian consult, a dental referral for the dentures, and staff assistance with meals. For the orthostatic hypotension, I am reducing lisinopril from 20 mg to 10 mg daily. I am discontinuing metformin because of his reduced kidney function and poor intake, and his A1c does not require another agent. I will continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day for atrial fibrillation and donepezil 5 mg daily, with delirium precautions. We discussed goals of care with the patient and his daughter, who prefer to avoid colonoscopy or other invasive testing, and I am requesting a palliative care consult. Physical and occupational therapy will see him, and I will repeat a basic metabolic panel tomorrow.
summary: An 87-year-old man with mild dementia, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease was on hospital day 3 for weakness, poor oral intake, and a fall, with his daughter providing much of the history. She clarified his weight loss as 22 pounds over 6 months and corrected his home lisinopril dose to 20 mg daily. He was frail with a drop in standing blood pressure, and imaging showed no mass. The assessment was frailty with multifactorial unintentional weight loss and orthostatic hypotension. The plan included starting mirtazapine, nutrition support, reducing lisinopril to 10 mg, stopping metformin, and a palliative care consult.

Reason for consult: duration of anticoagulation for a left leg deep vein thrombosis. Requesting service: primary care.

History of present illness: This is an 80-year-old female who developed a proximal left leg deep vein thrombosis about 11 weeks ago, after a hospitalization for pneumonia with several days of bed rest. She was started on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and has not missed any doses. Her leg swelling has improved. She denies bleeding, black stools, new leg swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She has no history of previous clots or cancer.

Examination: Blood pressure 128/76, HR 70, SpO2 97% on room air. There is mild residual swelling of the left calf, about 1 cm larger than the right, without tenderness, warmth, or redness.

Data reviewed: Hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 238, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. The duplex ultrasound at diagnosis showed thrombus in the left femoral vein.

Impression: Provoked left leg deep vein thrombosis that is improving on apixaban, with a major transient risk factor (hospitalization with immobility) and no bleeding on therapy.

Recommendations: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily to complete a total of 3 months, then stop. Repeat a duplex ultrasound of the left leg before stopping to document the residual clot. No thrombophilia testing is needed. Counsel on bleeding precautions and return precautions for new swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Hematology follow-up only if symptoms recur.
summary: An 80-year-old woman was seen in the specialty clinic at the request of primary care about how long to continue anticoagulation for a left leg deep vein thrombosis that developed about 11 weeks ago after a hospitalization for pneumonia. She takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily without missed doses, her leg swelling has improved, and she denies bleeding, black stools, new leg swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Examination showed mild residual swelling of the left calf without tenderness, warmth, or redness. The impression was a provoked deep vein thrombosis improving on apixaban, and the recommendation was to complete 3 months of apixaban, repeat a duplex ultrasound before stopping, and follow up only if symptoms recur.

Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 50-year-old male with lung cancer on pembrolizumab, here before your next treatment. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Honestly, tired. I am exhausted all the time, and I feel cold even when everyone else is warm. I have gained a few pounds too.
Doctor: How long has that been going on?
Patient: About three weeks.
Doctor: Any diarrhea or belly pain?
Patient: No diarrhea, no belly pain.
Doctor: Any new rash or itching?
Patient: No rash.
Doctor: Any headaches or vision changes?
Patient: No.
Doctor: How about your breathing? Any coughing up blood?
Patient: I have my usual dry cough, but no blood, and my breathing is the same as before.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 118/72, pulse 56, temperature 97.6, and oxygen is 96% on room air. Your lungs are clear, the thyroid is not enlarged or tender, and your skin is dry without a rash. Your blood work shows a TSH of 14.8, which is high, and a low free T4 of 0.6. Your hemoglobin is 12.9 and creatinine is 0.9, both fine. The CT of the chest from last week shows the mass in the right upper lobe has shrunk from 4.1 to 3.2 cm, so the cancer is responding.
Patient: That is good news. What about the tiredness?
Doctor: The tiredness is from an underactive thyroid caused by the immunotherapy. It is a known side effect and it is treatable. I am starting levothyroxine 50 micrograms every morning on an empty stomach. We will continue pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks, and today's treatment can go ahead. I will recheck the TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks. Call us right away if you get diarrhea, a rash, worse shortness of breath, or a severe headache.
Patient: Okay, I will.
summary: A 50-year-old man with lung cancer on pembrolizumab came in before his next treatment with about three weeks of tiredness, feeling cold, and a few pounds of weight gain. He denied diarrhea, belly pain, rash, headaches, vision changes, and coughing up blood, and he reported his usual dry cough. TSH was 14.8 with a low free T4 of 0.6, and CT showed the right upper lobe mass had shrunk from 4.1 to 3.2 cm. The clinician diagnosed an underactive thyroid caused by the immunotherapy, started levothyroxine 50 micrograms every morning, continued pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks, and planned to recheck thyroid tests in 6 weeks.

soap.subjective: 50-year-old male with lung cancer on pembrolizumab, here before his next treatment, with about three weeks of tiredness, feeling cold, and a few pounds of weight gain. TSH 14.8 (high), free T4 0.6 (low), hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 0.9. CT of the chest from last week shows the right upper lobe mass decreased from 4.1 to 3.2 cm.
soap.assessment: Lung cancer responding to pembrolizumab; underactive thyroid caused by the immunotherapy, accounting for the tiredness.
plan: Start levothyroxine 50 micrograms every morning on an empty stomach
Continue pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks; today's treatment can go ahead
Recheck TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks
Call right away for diarrhea, a rash, worse shortness of breath, or a severe headache

note:
Doctor: Come on in. I see you are a 58-year-old male here for a follow-up of your right wrist fracture. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: I fell off a ladder about three weeks ago and broke my wrist, the radius. They fixed it with a plate and I stayed in the hospital for two nights. The orthopedic clinic cannot see me until next week, and for the past few days my hand has been numb at night.
Doctor: So you had an ORIF, an open reduction and internal fixation, and you were discharged about three weeks ago. Where is the numbness?
Patient: My thumb, pointer finger, and middle finger. It wakes me up at night. And the wrist is more swollen than it was last week.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills.
Doctor: Any drainage or redness around the incision?
Patient: No drainage, no redness.
Doctor: Do your fingers ever turn blue or cold?
Patient: No, they stay pink.
Doctor: Any calf pain, chest pain, or trouble breathing since the surgery? We worry about blood clots after an operation.
Patient: No calf pain, no chest pain, and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: Good. You also have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let us go over your medicines.
Patient: I take metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, lisinopril 20 mg once a day for my pressure, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg every morning. From the hospital I got oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours.
Doctor: Okay. How often are you using the oxycodone?
Patient: Only at night now, one or two a day. Oh wait, I looked at the metformin bottle this morning and it says 1000 mg twice a day, not 500. I misspoke.
Doctor: Good catch. So the metformin is 1000 mg twice a day, and we will keep it that way. Now, your vital signs today: blood pressure 136/84, pulse 80, temperature 98.3, and oxygen 98% on room air. I took the splint off. The incision is clean and dry, it is healing well, and there is no redness or drainage. The wrist is mildly swollen. You have decreased sensation in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, your Phalen test is positive, and your fingers are warm with a brisk capillary refill and a good radial pulse. The X-ray we took today shows the distal radius fracture with the plate and screws in good position, the alignment is maintained, and there is early callus. Your hospital labs at discharge showed an A1c of 7.4 percent and a creatinine of 1.0.
Patient: So is it healing okay?
Doctor: The bone is healing well. The numbness is most likely carpal tunnel syndrome from swelling after the fracture and surgery. I am calling the orthopedic on-call doctor to move your appointment up to within the next two days. In the meantime, I am stopping the oxycodone because you only need it at night, and I am increasing the acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 8 hours. Continue the other medicines the same. Please wear this removable wrist splint at night in a neutral position, keep your hand raised above your heart, and do your finger exercises. If the numbness becomes constant, your fingers turn pale or cold, or you get a fever or drainage from the incision, go to the emergency room.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux came to urgent care about three weeks after plate fixation of a right distal radius fracture, reporting nighttime numbness in the thumb, pointer, and middle fingers and increasing wrist swelling. He denied fever, chills, incision drainage or redness, calf pain, chest pain, and trouble breathing, and he corrected his metformin dose to 1000 mg twice a day. The incision was clean, sensation was decreased in three fingers, and the X-ray showed good plate position. The clinician diagnosed likely carpal tunnel syndrome, stopped oxycodone, increased acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 8 hours, and arranged a night splint and expedited orthopedic follow-up.

Has type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux. Takes metformin 1000 mg twice a day (corrected from his first statement of 500 mg after checking the bottle), lisinopril 20 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg every morning, plus oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed (now only at night) and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours from the hospital.

X-ray shows the distal radius fracture with the plate and screws in good position, alignment maintained, and early callus. Hospital labs at discharge: A1c 7.4 percent, creatinine 1.0.

note:
This is a hospital day 3 progress note for gynecology, dictated. The patient is a 26-year-old female admitted two days ago with abnormal uterine bleeding and symptomatic anemia. She has had irregular, prolonged vaginal bleeding for about 3 weeks, which became heavy over the last 4 days with her soaking a pad every hour, along with lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations. Her history includes polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity, and asthma. She smokes one pack per day, correction, she smokes half a pack per day, about 10 cigarettes, for 6 years.

In the emergency department she was tachycardic with a heart rate of 118 and a blood pressure of 96/58. Hemoglobin was 6.8 g/dL, platelets 312, INR 1.0, TSH 2.4, and ferritin was very low. Urine hCG was negative. She received 2 units of packed red blood cells and her hemoglobin this morning is 8.6 g/dL. Pelvic ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus with an endometrial thickness of 9 mm and no fibroids or polyps, and the ovaries have multiple small peripheral follicles consistent with polycystic ovary syndrome.

Her home medications are metformin 500 mg twice a day, an albuterol inhaler as needed, and naproxen 500 mg twice a day for cramps. I discontinued the naproxen on admission while a bleeding disorder is being excluded. She has mild cramping but denies pelvic pain. She denies fever, chest pain, fainting, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and easy bruising.

On admission she was started on norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times a day, and the bleeding has slowed to light spotting. This morning her blood pressure is 112/68, heart rate 86, temperature 98.2 F, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 99% on room air. She looks less pale. Her abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no rebound, and there is light spotting on the pad. Pelvic exam was deferred.

Impression. Abnormal uterine bleeding most likely from ovulatory dysfunction related to polycystic ovary syndrome, with symptomatic anemia from blood loss and iron deficiency, improving. A bleeding disorder is less likely, but a von Willebrand panel has been sent. Tobacco use.

For the plan, one, reduce norethindrone acetate to 5 mg twice a day starting tonight, and 5 mg once daily at discharge for 3 months. Two, start ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice daily, and I will recheck the hemoglobin tomorrow. Three, continue to hold naproxen. Four, start a nicotine patch 14 mg daily based on half a pack per day, and I counseled her on quitting for 5 minutes and she accepted the patch. Five, continue metformin 500 mg twice a day and the albuterol inhaler as needed. Six, follow up the von Willebrand panel, and consider an endometrial biopsy in the outpatient gynecology clinic because of her polycystic ovary syndrome and obesity. Seven, anticipate discharge tomorrow if the hemoglobin is stable and the bleeding remains light.

note:
Telehealth video visit. The patient joined from home on a smartphone, his identity and location were confirmed verbally, and he consented to a video visit. He provided home-measured vitals.

Chief complaint: iron-deficiency anemia found on routine labs.

This is a 26-year-old male referred by his primary care clinician for evaluation of iron-deficiency anemia. Labs from 2 weeks ago showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, MCV 72, ferritin 7, and a negative tTG-IgA. He reports about 3 months of mild fatigue and dizziness when standing quickly, and he has intermittent burning discomfort in the upper abdomen after meals. He has been taking ibuprofen 600 mg about three times a week for tension headaches. He denies black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, weight loss, diarrhea, and difficulty swallowing. He eats a mostly vegetarian diet and does not donate blood. There is no family history of colon cancer.

Home-measured vitals: blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 72, temperature 98.1 F. On the video exam he appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences. Mild conjunctival pallor is visible. There is no jaundice. He palpated his own abdomen as directed and reports no tenderness or masses.

Impression: iron-deficiency anemia in a young man with no clear source yet, with upper abdominal burning that may be related to his regular ibuprofen use. I will schedule an EGD with duodenal biopsies and a colonoscopy to look for a source of blood loss. I am ordering a Helicobacter pylori stool antigen. He should stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for headaches instead. I am starting omeprazole 20 mg daily for 8 weeks and ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily. We will repeat the CBC and ferritin in 8 weeks and follow up by video after the endoscopy. He should seek care urgently for black stools, vomiting blood, chest pain, or fainting.

Home vitals were unremarkable, and the video exam showed mild conjunctival pallor without jaundice. The clinician planned an EGD with duodenal biopsies, a colonoscopy, and a Helicobacter pylori stool antigen, stopped ibuprofen, and started omeprazole and ferrous sulfate with repeat labs in 8 weeks.

note:
The patient is a 65-year-old male seen in the outpatient psychiatry clinic for follow-up of generalized anxiety disorder. He was accompanied by his daughter, who helps manage his medications and provided part of the history.

He reports persistent worry about his finances and his health that he finds hard to control, along with restlessness, muscle tension in his neck and shoulders, and difficulty falling asleep most nights. He tends to minimize his symptoms. His daughter adds that over the last two months he has been pacing at night, calling her several times a day to ask the same worries, and avoiding social events. He denies panic attacks, depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and alcohol use. He also denies chest pain and palpitations. His daughter has not seen him drink alcohol.

Current medications are sertraline 50 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime, which he has used most nights for the past year. His daughter notes that he sometimes takes a second lorazepam tablet when he cannot sleep.

On examination, blood pressure was 138/82 and heart rate 78. He was well groomed and cooperative, with an anxious affect, normal speech, and linear thinking, and he was fully oriented with intact memory on a brief screen. There was no suicidal or psychotic thinking. The GAD-7 score was 15 and the PHQ-9 score was 6. TSH was 1.9 and sodium 139 on labs from last month.

Assessment is generalized anxiety disorder that is only partially treated on a low dose of sertraline, with anxiety-related insomnia. Long-term lorazepam use is a concern in an older adult because of fall risk and effects on memory. Hypertension is controlled on lisinopril.

We will increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg daily. I will start a gradual taper off lorazepam, reducing to 0.25 mg at bedtime for two weeks and then stopping, and I explained the reasons to him and his daughter and gave her a written schedule. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. I referred him for cognitive behavioral therapy. We will recheck his sodium level four weeks after the sertraline increase and see him back in the clinic then.
summary: A 65-year-old man with generalized anxiety disorder was seen in psychiatry clinic with his daughter, who helped provide the history, reporting persistent worry about finances and health, restlessness, muscle tension, and difficulty falling asleep, with nighttime pacing. He denied panic attacks, depressed mood, suicidal ideation, chest pain, and palpitations, and he takes sertraline 50 mg, lisinopril, and lorazepam at bedtime, sometimes taking a second tablet. The GAD-7 score was 15 and the PHQ-9 score was 6. The clinician assessed partially treated generalized anxiety disorder with anxiety-related insomnia and a lorazepam concern in an older adult. Sertraline was increased to 100 mg daily, a lorazepam taper was started, and therapy referral and 4-week follow-up were arranged.

note:
This is a dictation for an emergency department visit. The patient is a 29-year-old male brought in by a friend with swelling of the lips and tongue and trouble breathing after eating. He has limited health literacy, so I used simple words, avoided medical terms, and checked his understanding with teach-back throughout the visit.

History of present illness. About 40 minutes before arrival he ate a shrimp stir-fry at a restaurant. He says the first symptoms started after about 20 minutes, correction, his friend says it was within 10 minutes of the first few bites, so symptom onset was within 10 minutes of eating. He developed an itchy mouth, then swelling of the lips and tongue, hives on his chest and arms, a tight throat, and a hoarse voice. He has eaten shrimp before with only a mild itchy mouth and did not know that was a warning sign. He denies vomiting, abdominal cramping, fainting, and chest pain. He has no known drug allergies, no new medications, and no insect stings.

Past history and medications. He has asthma, hypertension, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. He told me he takes cetirizine 20 mg daily, correction, I looked at the box he brought and it says 10 mg once daily. He also takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and an albuterol inhaler as needed.

Exam. On arrival his blood pressure was 142/88, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 94% on room air, and temperature 98.9 F. He was anxious, with visible swelling of the lips and tongue, diffuse hives on the chest and arms, a hoarse voice, and mild expiratory wheezing, and no stridor. His heart was fast and regular.

ED course. He received epinephrine 0.3 mg intramuscularly in the thigh within minutes of arrival, and a second dose of 0.3 mg after 10 minutes because the lip swelling persisted. He also received diphenhydramine 50 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV, and an albuterol nebulizer 2.5 mg for the wheezing. Within an hour the swelling and hives improved and the wheezing resolved. After treatment his blood pressure was 126/78, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 98% on room air. Labs showed WBC 9.8, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, potassium 4.0, and creatinine 1.0, and a serum tryptase was sent. He was observed for 6 hours with no return of symptoms.

Impression. Acute allergic reaction with angioedema and hives, most likely from shrimp, meeting criteria for anaphylaxis and responding to epinephrine. His lisinopril may also be contributing, since lisinopril can cause angioedema on its own and can make anaphylaxis harder to treat.

For the plan, one, discharge him with an epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg to use for any future reaction, and I demonstrated it with a trainer pen and he repeated the steps back correctly. Two, prednisone 40 mg daily for 3 days. Three, increase cetirizine from 10 mg daily to 10 mg twice daily for 5 days. Four, famotidine 20 mg twice daily for 3 days. Five, discontinue lisinopril and start amlodipine 5 mg daily for his blood pressure. Six, avoid shrimp and all shellfish, and refer him to an allergy clinic for follow-up. Seven, I gave him a picture-based instruction sheet, and he should call 911 or return right away for lip or tongue swelling, trouble breathing, or fainting. Eight, see his primary care clinician in 3 days to recheck his blood pressure on the new medicine.
summary: A 29-year-old man with asthma, hypertension, and seasonal allergic rhinitis, and limited health literacy, presented to the emergency department after eating shrimp with lip and tongue swelling, hives, a tight throat, a hoarse voice, and mild wheezing that began within 10 minutes. He denied vomiting, abdominal cramping, fainting, and chest pain, and arrival SpO2 was 94% on room air with heart rate 112. He improved after two doses of epinephrine, diphenhydramine, famotidine, methylprednisolone, and an albuterol nebulizer, with no recurrence over 6 hours. The impression was an allergic reaction with angioedema meeting anaphylaxis criteria, most likely from shrimp. He went home with an epinephrine auto-injector, prednisone, higher-dose cetirizine, and famotidine, with lisinopril replaced by amlodipine and allergy follow-up arranged.
